Eggs of the White-starred robin (Pogonocichla stellata) are typically incubated at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C], and under these conditions hatching occurs after approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days]. This incubation period is consistent with the values reported for many other small-bodied African montane forest passerines. Upon emerging, the hatchlings exhibit a wet weight at birth of 2.5 grams [Wwb = 2.5 grams], a modest mass that reflects the altricial developmental mode characteristic of many turdids. The initial wet weight of the newly laid egg, before any significant metabolic expenditure, has been recorded at 3.05 grams [Ww0 = 3.05 grams]. This value indicates that the egg represents a substantial maternal investment, and the chick's birth mass relative to the egg mass suggests a relatively efficient conversion of yolk reserves into embryonic tissue. The environment within the nest cup is closely regulated by the attending adults, maintaining the stable temperature necessary for normal embryogenesis and hatching success.

Fledging marks a critical developmental transition in Pogonocichla stellata. At the body temperature typical of an active, endothermic nestling, which is approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], young birds leave the nest after 14 days following hatching [tx = 14 days following hatching]. This relatively short nestling period is advantageous for a species that nests in exposed edge habitats, as it reduces the window of vulnerability to predation. The timing is remarkably consistent with the fledging ages observed in other montane robins of equivalent adult body size. The achievement of flight at this age permits the fledgling to escape terrestrial predators and begin exploring the understory. During the final days in the nest, the chick undergoes a rapid phase of feather growth and mass gain, preparing it for the energetic demands of independent locomotion. Parental provisioning continues for several weeks after nest departure, gradually declining as the juvenile becomes more proficient at foraging on its own.

Sexual maturation in the White-starred robin proceeds according to a predictable schedule under standard thermal conditions. When the operative body temperature is maintained at approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at puberty for males and females is roughly 42 days [tp = roughly 42 days]. This rapid attainment of reproductive maturity is noteworthy for a relatively long-lived passerine and may be an adaptation to unpredictable breeding opportunities in montane environments where productive seasons are brief. The maturation timeline aligns well with the pattern of early gonad development seen in several other forest robins, although it is somewhat accelerated compared to species occupying more stable, lowland tropical forests. Following puberty, adults commence the process of pair formation and territory establishment. The first successful breeding event, however, does not occur immediately; there is typically a substantial gap between reaching physiological maturity and initiating reproduction, a period used for acquiring a breeding territory and a mate.

The age at which Pogonocichla stellata initiates its first breeding attempt has been documented under field conditions at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], again referencing the species' active metabolic body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This deferred first reproduction, coming almost a full year after the individual has become sexually mature, is a life-history strategy common among small passerines that must compete for high-quality territories in saturated montane habitats. The reproductive output during this first breeding event is typically modest. Females lay 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per clutch], and field records indicate that generally only a single clutch is produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch is produced each year]. This annual rhythm is likely constrained by the length of the favorable breeding season in the highlands, which may be too short to allow for successful replacement or second clutches. The combination of a moderate clutch size and a single annual nesting attempt results in a relatively low overall reproductive rate for a bird of this body size.

Maximum lifespan estimates for Pogonocichla stellata, derived from a comparative analysis using the well-studied song thrush Turdus philomelos as a reference, suggest a longevity of approximately 6,389 days [am = approximately 6,389 days] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This corresponds to roughly 17.5 years, placing the species among the longer-lived members of the Muscicapidae. Achieving such longevity is contingent upon the consistent availability of food resources and the avoidance of predation, which is a considerable challenge for a bird that forages on the forest floor. The ultimate wet weight for adult females is 20.2 grams [Wwi = 20.2 grams], while males reach a slightly larger adult body mass of 21.4 grams [Wwi = 21.4 grams]. This modest degree of sexual size dimorphism is typical of socially monogamous passerines with biparental care, where selection pressures on male size are less extreme than in polygynous systems. The energetic demands of achieving these adult body masses, combined with the species' relatively long lifespan, shape a life history characterized by conservative reproductive investment and high adult survival.
